classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate twice, then use the exponential velocity law to sketch its approach to a limiting value and justify why it never reaches zero.

content.prompt: The position $x$ cm of a particle moving along an $x$-axis is given by $x=5t+e^{-2t}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the initial position, velocity and acceleration of the particle.

answer.short: The curve rises from $(0,3)$ and approaches $v=5$ from below.
answer.worked: Plot $v=5-2e^{-2t}$ for $t\ge 0$. The intercept is $(0,3)$. The gradient $4e^{-2t}$ is positive and decreases towards zero, so the curve rises and levels off towards $v=5$.

spec.sourceRegion: Answer book printed page 357, P2(b), upper left
spec.description: Velocity–time graph with the printed 1–3 second ticks, 1–5 velocity ticks and a light major grid. The source blue series is represented with standard booklet blue.
spec.mathematics: v=5-2e^{-2t} for t≥0. The curve starts at (0,3), increases with decreasing gradient and approaches 5 from below. Major grid increments are 1 second and 1 cm/s.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Will the particle ever come to rest? Explain.

answer.short: No. The velocity is always at least $3\ \text{cm/s}$ and approaches $5\ \text{cm/s}$.
answer.worked: For $t\ge 0$, $0<e^{-2t}\le 1$. Hence $3\le 5-2e^{-2t}<5$, so $v(t)>0$ at every time and the particle never comes to rest.
